scope: These notes use several retained interviews and retrospective accounts, credited separately for each track. Memories, editorial explanations and official discography statements are distinguished; they are not a complete master-recording history or independent audio analysis. Questions are optional.

entries.description: Prince wanted the song less frantic and decided to record it again, engineer Susan Rogers recalls in Mix. Her account describes a drum-machine foundation playing back while Prince and the band performed live with their instruments connected directly.

sourceLabels.https://www.mixonline.com/recording/lets: Mix classic-track production history with engineer Susan Rogers

entries.question: How do the live parts seem to sit against the drum-machine foundation?

entries.description: Lisa Coleman recalls doubling Apollonia's vocals on this song in SPIN's Purple Rain oral history. Apollonia's response in that account is less certain: she does not remember the doubling, though she imagines Coleman is on the recording.

sourceLabels.https://www.spinmagazine.com/2016/04/pri: SPIN oral history with Lisa Coleman and Apollonia Kotero

entries.description: Susan Rogers remembered the song as personally important to Prince. Rolling Stone quotes her 1989 account saying it was written for Susannah Melvoin and meant a great deal to him.

sourceLabels.https://www.rollingstone.com/music/music: Rolling Stone account quoting engineer Susan Rogers

entries.description: Wendy Melvoin describes a passage in which she has to follow Prince's playing exactly. In her Guitar.com interview, she says the fingering remains awkward for her and the final triplet demands extra concentration.

sourceLabels.https://guitar.com/features/interviews/t: Guitar.com interview with Wendy Melvoin and Lisa Coleman

entries.question: Can you find a passage where the guitar lines seem closely coordinated, and what helps you follow them?

entries.description: “Darling Nikki” connects two very different accounts. Susan Rogers tells Tape Op it was the first tape Prince asked her to rough-mix after she finished his home-studio installation. TIME traces Tipper Gore's concern about record disclaimers to hearing the song with her daughter, then describes the formation of the Parents Music Resource Center in 1985.

sourceLabels.https://tapeop.com/interviews/117/susan-: Tape Op interview with engineer Susan Rogers
sourceLabels.https://time.com/4303801/prince-dead-dar: TIME history of Darling Nikki and parental advisory labels

entries.description: A missing part is central to the recording's documented design. The Library of Congress describes Prince dropping the bass line to create the song's distinctive sound.

sourceLabels.https://www.loc.gov/programs/national-re: Library of Congress National Recording Registry description

entries.question: Without a bass line, what draws your attention to the rhythm?

entries.description: Asked about the sequencer-like pattern, Susan Rogers identifies Matt Fink in her Tape Op interview. She says the track was cut live and that Fink programmed the part.

sourceLabels.https://tapeop.com/interviews/117/susan-: Tape Op interview with engineer Susan Rogers

entries.question: Does the sequencer-like pattern hold your attention as a repeating figure, or recede behind other parts?

entries.description: Prince's official discography places the band's first performance of this song at the First Avenue benefit, alongside “Purple Rain” and “I Would Die 4 U.”

Lisa Coleman recalls working with Prince on the live recording in a Los Angeles studio. The Guardian's account adds that strings were overdubbed and the recording was edited from thirteen minutes to eight minutes and forty-one seconds.
